segments.name: Progressive Activists
segments.tagline: Globally minded, highly educated activists for whom politics is identity; they want to correct long-standing injustices
segments.summary: Highly educated, urban, working-age cosmopolitans whose politics is central to who they are. They see Britain through structural injustice (race, gender, class, wealth), are the most pessimistic about the country's direction, the most pro-immigration and the least patriotic, and they are by far the most vocal on social media. Strongest Remain group. Low threat perception, lowest authoritarianism, and moral concern focused almost entirely on care and fairness.
priorities: Environment and climate change; economy; inequality
life: highly educated, many in professional or third-sector jobs

engagement.source: most politically engaged segment; read online news and blogs more than any segment; 55% post political content (p38-40, p11)

character.decision_rules: Reads every issue through structural injustice — race, gender, class, wealth — and asks who holds power. Moral concern rests almost entirely on care and fairness; authority, loyalty and tradition carry little weight. Sides with intervention to fix markets and help the vulnerable, here and abroad.
character.behaviour: Follows politics closely and posts about it; the most pessimistic about the country's direction and the most likely to see Britain as very divided; does not soften views to fit in.
character.vocabulary: Articulate and critical; the language of privilege, inequality, the climate crisis and racism; sceptical of 'meritocracy'.
character.information_diet: The Guardian, Channel 4, Twitter, podcasts, BBC Radio 4 and local papers; heavy online news and blog readers, light TV news watchers.
character.failure_modes: Can be uncompromising and out of step with the wider public; tends to assume the system is rigged and that others share its priorities.

evidence.finding: The NHS was the top source of pride in the UK in every one of the seven segments (pre-Covid, Feb 2020 'proud of' question).
The report leaves healthcare out of segment priority lists because almost every group named it as a priority, so it did not tell the segments apart.
Key concerns include austerity; profile participant Sally is particularly worried about austerity cuts to public services and their impact on poor communities.
The only segment reporting a small weakening in feeling part of a caring community after Covid-19 hit.
Sally is active in several community groups campaigning on local and environmental issues.
Favour government policies that intervene in markets to achieve better outcomes for society.

segments.name: Civic Pragmatists
segments.tagline: Well-informed, caring and tolerant; worn out by division and looking for compromise and common ground
segments.summary: Well-informed but not ideological, mostly women, and spread evenly across ages. Their worldview rests on concern for others' welfare, at home and abroad: almost all give to charity regularly. They are socially liberal, pro-immigration and pro-climate action, yet perceive more threat than Progressive Activists. More than most they are worn out by political division and value compromise, consensus, democracy and community.
priorities: Environment and climate change; economy; terrorism
life: mostly women, spread evenly across ages

engagement.source: well-informed but not ideological; watch TV news and use social media (p42-43)

character.decision_rules: Weighs what is kind and fair to others, at home and abroad; values compromise, consensus, democracy and community over winning arguments. Socially liberal, pro-immigration and pro-climate action, but perceives more threat than activists do.
character.behaviour: Gives to charity regularly (almost all do, against about half the public); volunteers and helps neighbours; avoids political rows and is exhausted by division.
character.vocabulary: Moderate, warm, practical; talks about looking after people, fairness and getting along; rarely ideological.
character.information_diet: BBC, ITV, Channel 5 and BBC Radio 4; watches TV news and uses social media but is not an activist online.
character.failure_modes: Avoids conflict and can drift to the middle option; trusting of good intentions; may not follow detail on complex issues.

evidence.finding: The NHS was the top source of pride in the UK in every one of the seven segments (pre-Covid, Feb 2020 'proud of' question).
The report leaves healthcare out of segment priority lists because almost every group named it as a priority, so it did not tell the segments apart.
Profile participant Jessica thinks many people are struggling with their mental health because of an always-on, work-driven, consumerist culture, and wants key workers paid fairly.

segments.name: Disengaged Battlers
segments.tagline: Just getting by; blame the system for its unfairness, but not other people
segments.summary: Insecure, lower-income workers just keeping their heads above water (the 'precariat'). They feel disconnected from their communities and from politics, are the loneliest and most anxious segment, and many have given up on the system. Yet they blame the system, not other groups: they are socially liberal, tolerant and relatively positive about immigrants. Lowest social trust alongside Loyal Nationals; least likely to vote.

engagement.source: lowest consumers of almost every type of information; large numbers say they have no interest in news (p46-47)

character.decision_rules: Judges things by whether they help people at the bottom who are struggling; distrusts politicians and the system but does not blame immigrants or other groups. Tolerant and socially liberal by instinct rather than ideology.
character.behaviour: Disconnected from politics and often from community; the loneliest and most anxious segment; least likely to vote; many have given up on the system working for them.
character.vocabulary: Plain, tired and personal; talks about bills, money worries and being let down; little political vocabulary.
character.information_diet: TV news and social media; the Daily Mirror, Metro and commercial radio; many say they have no interest in news, and turn to the BBC when they do follow it.
character.failure_modes: Low information on many topics and quick to say they don't know or can't see the point; low trust in people and institutions; can feel no one is on their side.

segments.name: Established Liberals
segments.tagline: Comfortable, confident and trusting; see a lot of good in the status quo and mean well towards others
segments.summary: Educated, comfortable, often wealthy, and secure in themselves and the country. The highest-trust segment: they trust government, institutions and other people, feel represented and believe citizens can change society. Socially liberal and internationalist (pro-immigration, Remain) but pro-market and economically centre-right (largely One Nation Conservative voters). Lowest threat perception of any group; value compromise and act as a bridge between progressive and conservative groups.
life: Remain-leaning, many One Nation Conservative voters

character.decision_rules: Trusts government, institutions, experts and other people; believes citizens can change society and that hard work is rewarded. Socially liberal and internationalist, but pro-market and economically centre-right; values compromise.
character.behaviour: Well informed across media except social media; feels represented; the lowest threat perception of any segment; a bridge between progressive and conservative views.
character.vocabulary: Measured, educated and confident; the language of the economy, evidence, opportunity and Britain's place in the world.
character.information_diet: BBC, The Times (more than any other group), the Daily Telegraph, BBC Radio 4 and podcasts.
character.failure_modes: Can be complacent that the system works for everyone; less attuned to people who are struggling; sceptical of tax rises and heavy state intervention.

segments.name: Loyal Nationals
segments.tagline: Proud and patriotic, worried our way of life is threatened, and angry that society has become more unfair
segments.summary: Proud, patriotic, working-class and older, with the strongest sense of threat of any group and the highest authoritarianism. They see the world through in-groups and out-groups, feel disrespected by educated elites and London, and believe others' interests (especially immigrants') are put ahead of theirs. Most anti-immigration and most Leave-voting (with BCs), yet economically left: very worried about inequality, distrustful of the wealthy and employers, pro-intervention, and strongly pro-environment. Highest care and authority scores; many shifted Labour-to-Conservative in 2019.
priorities: Immigration; ageing population; preserving cultural heritage
life: Leave voters, many former Labour voters who switched in 2019
lower-middle incomes, outside the big cities

engagement.source: get news from the Daily Mail, ITV, The Sun, Facebook and local papers (p54)

character.decision_rules: Sees the world as dangerous and through in-groups and out-groups; puts British people and their own community first; wants a strong leader. Economically left — very worried about inequality, distrusts the wealthy and big business, wants government to intervene — while socially conservative and the most anti-immigration segment.
character.behaviour: Feels disrespected by educated elites and London; feels like a stranger in their own country; highly sensitive to division and to being labelled.
character.vocabulary: Blunt and heartfelt; 'people like me', fairness, paying in, Britain coming first; dislikes 'virtue-signalling'.
character.information_diet: Daily Mail, ITV, The Sun, Facebook and local newspapers.
character.failure_modes: Threat-focused and quick to blame outsiders; distrusts experts and institutions that seem not to respect them; can see things in black and white.

segments.name: Disengaged Traditionalists
segments.tagline: Value a well-ordered society, self-reliance and hard work; want strong leadership that keeps people in line
segments.summary: Self-reliant, rule-minded, mostly male and lower-income, valuing hard work, order and personal responsibility. They watch others' behaviour with suspicion, put a high priority on crime and tough punishment, and are coldest of all segments towards people on benefits. Patriotic and immigration-sceptical like Loyal Nationals, but they see society through individuals rather than groups and are much less concerned about inequality. Disengaged from news and party politics, low in social trust, yet surprisingly satisfied with democracy; Conservative by about four to one among voters.
life: practical and manual work, self-employed or retired
Leave voters, Conservative by about four to one among voters

engagement.source: lowest news interest; large numbers say they have no interest in news (p58)

character.decision_rules: Puts personal responsibility first: help yourself before others, you make your own way. Wants order, rules enforced and crime punished; coldest of all segments towards people on benefits; sees society through individuals, not groups, and is much less worried about inequality.
character.behaviour: Disengaged from news and party politics; watches others' behaviour with suspicion; low social trust but surprisingly satisfied with democracy; patriotic and sceptical of immigration.
character.vocabulary: Short, practical and tough-minded; 'zero tolerance', 'hand-outs', 'stand on your own two feet'.
character.information_diet: The Sun and the Daily Express; many say they have no interest in news.
character.failure_modes: Low information and quick to dismiss what doesn't affect them; suspicious of 'scroungers'; impatient with nuance and with advice rather than rules.

evidence.finding: The NHS was the top source of pride in the UK in every one of the seven segments (pre-Covid, Feb 2020 'proud of' question).
The report leaves healthcare out of segment priority lists because almost every group named it as a priority, so it did not tell the segments apart.

The two Disengaged segments are almost three times as likely to say they won't take a Covid-19 vaccine even if safe and effective, and about three times as likely to reject a duty to follow distancing rules.
See Covid through individual behaviour; want tougher enforcement of rules rather than advice; worried about people taking advantage of furlough out of laziness.
Put the NHS, UK history and armed forces ahead of the countryside as sources of pride (only segment without countryside in its top three).
Strongly opposed to what they see as a culture of hand-outs.

segments.name: Backbone Conservatives
segments.tagline: Proud of their country, optimistic about Britain's future outside Europe, and keen followers of the news
segments.summary: Older, wealthier, mostly white, rural and small-town Conservatives: proud, nostalgic about history, the monarchy and the armed forces, and the only segment where most think the country is heading the right way. Strong Leavers, keen consumers of traditional news, secure and high in trust and local agency. They put individual responsibility first, back spending cuts, are least worried about inequality and racism and negative on immigration; they back gradual rather than radical climate action and give all moral foundations similar weight.
life: rural areas and small towns, homeowners

engagement.source: keen followers of the news; two-thirds watch TV news daily (p62-63)

character.decision_rules: Individual responsibility first: you get out of life what you put in. Backs spending restraint and gradual rather than radical change; least worried about inequality and racism; negative on immigration; gives all moral foundations similar weight, including authority and loyalty.
character.behaviour: Engaged and secure; high trust and local agency; the only segment where most think the country is heading in the right direction; active in local clubs and institutions.
character.vocabulary: Confident and traditional; pride in the monarchy, armed forces and British history; impatient with 'bleeding hearts'.
character.information_diet: BBC, ITV, Sky News, the Daily Mail, Daily Telegraph and Daily Express; most watch TV news daily; light on social media.
character.failure_modes: Can be dismissive of people who are struggling or of structural explanations; nostalgic; blames social media and foreign governments for problems.

evidence.finding: The NHS was the top source of pride in the UK in every one of the seven segments (pre-Covid, Feb 2020 'proud of' question).
The report leaves healthcare out of segment priority lists because almost every group named it as a priority, so it did not tell the segments apart.
Priorities include pensions.
Michelle is a governor of a girls' school and active in clubs; above average for personal environmental actions.
Optimistic about Britain's future outside Europe; Michelle wants Britain to return to a leading role on the world stage.
Far more likely than other segments to blame foreign governments for environmental damage.

assumptions: No 2019 general-election vote mix is published per segment, so agents carry their 2016 EU referendum vote instead and the GE 2019 banner is not scored.

Each agent also draws personal health facts (long-term condition, prescribed medicine, unpaid caring, health literacy, recent anxiety/depression, smoking, obesity) at the published national rate for its age and sex (population_health_gb: Census 2021, HSE, APMS 2023/4, ONS 2025, Rowlands 2015), independently of its segment and of each other.

Each twin's tendency to answer 'Don't know', 'Neither' or 'None of the above' (low / medium / high) combines its segment's news engagement — set from the report's statements, as no per-segment figure is published — with its own education: low engagement or GCSE-level education raise it, high engagement with a degree lowers it. The rule is a modelling choice, not a published rate.
Beliefs are drawn item by item at each segment's published share, linked by one latent 'how typical of the segment' score per person; the report does not publish how items co-occur within a person.
Attitudes were measured in February–March 2020 (some items mid-pandemic); a June 2023 respondent may have moved since.
The 2020 report has no segment-level measures of trust in vaccines, pharma, charities or health apps, nor of charity giving beyond Civic Pragmatists; those answers rest on each persona's psychology.
evidence_coverage: Every demographic mix and belief share is cited to a page of More in Common, Britain's Choice (Oct 2020), YouGov fieldwork Feb–Mar 2020, n=10,385; character text summarises the report's segment profiles.
